sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how regulated entities use AI and machine learning to strengthen transaction monitoring and suspicious activity detection, and the practical trade-offs supervisors should expect firms to manage.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-level supervisory and financial crime specialist staff assessing firms' financial crime controls.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain how AI/ML techniques are applied to transaction monitoring
- Describe network and graph analytics approaches to detecting suspicious activity
- Assess the trade-off between detection sensitivity and false-positive rates
- Evaluate a firm's AI-driven monitoring system for supervisory adequacy
- Identify the human oversight controls that should accompany AI-driven detection
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: AI/ML in transaction monitoring (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain AI/ML applications in transaction monitoring*
- From rules-based to AI/ML-driven transaction monitoring
- Anomaly detection and behavioural profiling techniques
- Network and graph analytics for detecting suspicious patterns
- Realistic capabilities and limitations of current AI/ML tools
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: AI adoption in AML systems participants have encountered

**Session 2: False positives and detection trade-offs (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess the sensitivity/false-positive trade-off*
- Why false-positive rates matter for both firms and supervisors
- Techniques for false-positive reduction and their risks
- The risk of tuning systems to minimise workload rather than maximise detection
- Assessing model performance metrics critically
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample AI monitoring system's performance metrics

**Session 3: Supervisory assessment and oversight (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate AI monitoring systems and identify oversight controls*
- Supervisory criteria for assessing AI-driven monitoring adequacy
- Human oversight and escalation controls that should accompany AI detection
- Case study: a firm's AI monitoring system under supervisory review
Activities:
- Case study: evaluate a firm's AI-driven monitoring system and identify oversight gaps

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: AI/ML techniques, false-positive trade-offs, oversight
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: AI/ML in transaction monitoring (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: False positives and detection trade-offs (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Supervisory assessment and oversight (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- AI/ML-driven monitoring changes the nature of supervisory review — from checking rules to assessing model performance
- Reducing false positives is only beneficial if genuine detection capability is preserved
- Human oversight remains essential even in highly automated detection systems

*Objective: Consolidate learning*

Activities:

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' practical skills in explainability techniques such as LIME and SHAP, which supervisors can use to assess whether firms' AI models are sufficiently auditable and transparent. Structure informed by EU-SDFA's published course on supervising and regulating AI in the financial sector.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-level supervisory staff building capability in AI-related supervision and internal AI use.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain why explainability matters for supervised AI models
- Describe the LIME and SHAP explainability techniques
- Assess whether a firm's approach to explainability is proportionate to the model's stakes
- Apply an explainability framework to a sample AI model output
- Evaluate the limitations of current explainability techniques
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Why explainability matters (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the importance of explainability*
- The 'black box' problem in complex AI models
- Why explainability matters for supervisory challenge and accountability
- Explainability versus interpretability: important distinctions
- Regulatory expectations around explainable AI
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: black-box model concerns participants have encountered

**Session 2: LIME and SHAP techniques (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe and apply LIME and SHAP*
- How LIME approximates model behaviour locally
- How SHAP allocates feature contribution using game-theoretic principles
- Practical demonstration of both techniques on a sample model output
- Choosing between explainability techniques for different model types
Activities:
- Exercise: apply LIME or SHAP-style analysis to a sample AI model output

**Session 3: Proportionality and limitations (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess proportionality and evaluate limitations*
- Matching explainability rigour to the stakes of the model's decisions
- Limitations: explainability techniques can themselves be imperfect approximations
- Case study: a firm's explainability approach under supervisory review
Activities:
- Case study: assess whether a firm's explainability approach is proportionate and adequate

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: why explainability matters, LIME/SHAP, proportionality
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Why explainability matters (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: LIME and SHAP techniques (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Proportionality and limitations (13:30–14:45)

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in supervising firms' algorithmic and high-frequency trading controls, including pre-trade risk controls and market-making obligations.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors working in investment services/capital markets supervision.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain algorithmic and high-frequency trading and their market role
- Describe pre-trade risk control requirements
- Assess a firm's algorithmic trading governance and testing framework
- Evaluate market-making obligations and their supervision
- Formulate a supervisory assessment of an algorithmic trading control framework
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Algorithmic and HFT fundamentals (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain algo/HFT trading and its market role*
- How algorithmic and high-frequency trading strategies operate
- Benefits and risks: liquidity provision versus flash-crash risk
- Regulatory concerns specific to algorithmic trading
- The evolving market share of algorithmic trading
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: algorithmic trading incidents participants are aware of

**Session 2: Pre-trade controls and governance (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe pre-trade controls and assess governance/testing*
- Pre-trade risk control requirements: limits, kill switches, circuit breakers
- Algorithm testing and approval governance
- Assessing whether controls are genuinely effective, not just present
- Common control failures in algorithmic trading
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample firm's algorithmic trading governance framework

**Session 3: Market-making obligations and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate market-making obligations and formulate an assessment*
- Market-making obligations under MiFID II and their supervision
- Assessing genuine liquidity provision versus opportunistic behaviour
- Case study: an algorithmic trading control framework under review
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of an algorithmic trading control framework

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: algo/HFT role, pre-trade controls, market-making obligations
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Algorithmic and HFT fundamentals (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Pre-trade controls and governance (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Market-making obligations and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Algorithmic trading controls must be tested for genuine effectiveness, not merely confirmed to exist
- Pre-trade risk controls are the first line of defence against algorithmic trading incidents
- Market-making obligations should be assessed against actual liquidity provision behaviour, not just formal commitments

sections.Syllabus:
**Block 1 | Workshop 1** — Understanding investment funds and the value chain Describe an investment fund, explain how it operates and identify pros and cons for investors Discuss how the investment fund market has developed in Malta and across the EU Explain the investment fund value chain from product development and distribution through to management, operations and administration Present a schema for investment fund regulation across the value chain

**Block 2 | Workshops 1–2** — Understanding supervisory risks and EU investment fund regulation Explain the key supervisory risks in funds and asset management Identify key parts of the EU’s framework of investment fund regulation that support supervisors in mitigating these risks Discuss the purpose of the UCITS Directive and explain the high-level rules applying to its management, operation and distribution Analyse whether the UCITS Directive has been effective in reducing harm caused by recent investment fund scandals Discuss the AIFM Directive and other EU regulations applicable to other types of investment fund

**Block 3 | Workshops 3–4** — Understanding cross-border fund rules and sustainable investment disclosures Explain the rules applicable to fund leverage, liquidity management and fund valuation Discuss cross-border fund regulation in the EU, including cross-border distribution, passporting, investor disclosure and investment services Explain how the EU’s regulation for sustainable finance applies to investment funds, including fund categorisation Discuss whether sustainable finance disclosure requirements are effective in preventing greenwashing/bleaching

**Block 4 | Workshop 4** — Understanding costs, charges and other regulatory topics Describe the regulation of costs levied by investment funds, including the prevention of undue costs being charged to investors Explain other EU regulation that indirectly applies to/influences funds (MiFID, DORA, SSR, AML, EMIR, etc.) Identify regulatory topics that will influence investment fund and asset management regulation going forward

**Session | Date** — Learning Objectives & Content

**Workshop 1 | 2 July 2024** — Today’s focus: what funds are, how the market works, and risk fundamentals Level-setting: what are funds and what is asset management Overview of the Maltese and EU investment fund and asset management market Introduction of the fund regulation ‘schema’: product, distribution, management, operations and admin Break-out group mapping of supervisory risk areas to the regulation schema Overview of EU fund regulation: UCITSD V+VI, AIFMD I+II, MMFR, ELTIF I+II/EuVECA/EuSEF Overview of cross-border fund distribution regulation: CBDFR/D and PRIIPs I+II

**Workshop 2 | 3 July 2024** — Today’s focus: UCITS Directive in depth Recap of Workshop 1 Overview of the UCITS Directive — why it exists, what it is, what it covers Deeper dive into management and product-related rules and guidance in the UCITS Directive Break-out case study (the ‘Woodford’ case): are the UCITS rules effective?

**Workshop 3 | 5 September 2024** — Today’s focus: AIFM Directive, leverage, liquidity and valuation Recap of the first two sessions Overview of the AIFM Directive I+II — why it exists, what it is, what it covers Overview of how fund leverage and liquidity are regulated, and what can go wrong Overview of investment fund valuation regulation and red flags to look out for Deeper dive into other EU fund regulations: MMFR, ELTIF I+II/EuVECA/EuSEF

**Workshop 4 | 25 September 2024** — Today’s focus: sustainable finance, cross-border distribution, costs and the regulatory horizon Recap of Workshop 3 Overview of cross-border fund regulation, including CBDFD/R and passporting Overview of sustainable finance regulation applicable to investment funds, including the SFDR Overview of disclosure regulations including PRIIPs and ESG-related disclosures; break-out discussion on greenwashing/bleaching Overview of regulation on undue costs for investment funds Overview of other EU regulation indirectly applying to funds: MiFID, DORA, SSR, AML, EMIR Forward look: emerging regulatory topics, including the EU’s Retail Investment Strategy proposals

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in assessing AI systems used in credit decisioning, insurance underwriting, and other financial services for bias and fairness, applying recognised testing methodologies.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-level supervisory staff building capability in AI-related supervision and internal AI use.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain how bias can enter AI systems used in credit and insurance decisions
- Describe recognised fairness testing methodologies
- Apply a fairness testing approach to a sample AI decisioning system
- Assess the trade-offs between different fairness definitions
- Formulate a supervisory assessment of bias risk in a financial AI system
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Bias in credit and insurance AI (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain how bias enters financial AI decisioning*
- Sources of bias in credit decisioning and insurance underwriting AI
- Historical data bias and its perpetuation through AI models
- Proxy discrimination: how models can encode bias indirectly
- The particular sensitivity of credit and insurance decisions
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: bias concerns in credit/insurance AI participants are aware of

**Session 2: Fairness testing methodologies (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe and apply fairness testing methodologies*
- Recognised fairness testing methodologies and metrics
- Testing for disparate impact across protected characteristics
- Practical demonstration of fairness testing on a sample dataset
- Data requirements and limitations for fairness testing
Activities:
- Exercise: apply a fairness testing approach to a sample credit decisioning model

**Session 3: Fairness trade-offs and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess fairness trade-offs and formulate an assessment*
- Why different fairness definitions can conflict with one another
- Choosing an appropriate fairness standard for a given use case
- Case study: a credit decisioning model raising fairness concerns
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of bias risk for a sample financial AI system

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: bias sources, fairness testing, trade-offs
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Bias in credit and insurance AI (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Fairness testing methodologies (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Fairness trade-offs and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Bias in credit and insurance AI can perpetuate historical discrimination even without explicit discriminatory intent
- Different fairness definitions can genuinely conflict, making the choice of standard a real policy decision
- Fairness testing should be an ongoing discipline throughout a model's lifecycle, not a one-off pre-launch check

- Case study: an authority's SupTech journey
Activities:
- Case study: design a phased SupTech capability-building plan

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: SupTech categories, build-versus-buy, skills, starting points
Activities:

- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: Equips supervisors to conduct business model analysis (BMA) as a core part of supervisory risk assessment: how firms develop corporate strategy and business models, why and how supervisors assess them, qualitative and quantitative analytical methods, and how to score and conclude a BMA assessment using a case study exercise.

- Explain the purpose of business model analysis for supervisors

sections.Syllabus:
**Morning | 09:30–12:30** — Level setting and theory What is corporate strategy and what is a business model? — firm characterisation, strategic questions, business model components Why look at business models — the purpose of BMA for supervisors and where strategy/business model risk fits in the supervisory risk framework Facets of business model and strategy risk, the value chain, organisation and management considerations How supervisors undertake BMA — roadmap, proportionality, preliminary assessment, information sources

**Early Afternoon | 13:30–14:30** — Qualitative and quantitative analysis Assessing the business environment: macro environment, competitive environment, supplier/buyer power, threat of new entrants and substitution Quantitative analysis: profitability KRIs, capital structure and quality, concentration risk Qualitative analysis: key dependencies and questions to challenge management assumptions Assessing strategy: why strategies fail, financial projections, execution risk, identifying key vulnerabilities

**Late Afternoon | 14:50–16:00** — Case study, assessment and scoring Case study exercise: SWOT analysis and strategy comparison of two contrasting fund administration businesses, followed by a supervisory assessment exercise Business model assessment and scoring: how to document vulnerabilities and score BMA outcomes (low / medium-low / medium-high / high risk) Review of management responses and discussion of how unexpected events can stress business models

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in assessing proposed changes of control and complex ownership structures, including cross-border and beneficial ownership considerations.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level authorisations/licensing caseworkers assessing new-entrant applications.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain what triggers a change-of-control assessment
- Describe the assessment criteria applied to a proposed new controller
- Assess beneficial ownership in complex or layered structures
- Evaluate cross-border ownership structures for transparency risk
- Formulate a change-of-control assessment outcome
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Change-of-control triggers and criteria (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain triggers and assessment criteria*
- What constitutes a notifiable change of control
- Assessment criteria for a proposed new controller
- Timelines and procedural requirements
- Interaction with fit-and-proper assessment
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: change-of-control cases participants have encountered

**Session 2: Beneficial ownership and complex structures (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess beneficial ownership in complex structures*
- Tracing beneficial ownership through layered structures
- Trusts, nominees, and other opacity-creating structures
- Red flags in ownership structures
- Tools and registries for verifying ownership
Activities:
- Exercise: trace beneficial ownership through a sample layered structure

**Session 3: Cross-border ownership and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate cross-border structures and formulate an assessment*
- Cross-border transparency risk
- Cooperating with foreign authorities on ownership verification
- Case study: a proposed change of control with a complex cross-border structure
Activities:
- Case study: assess a proposed change of control and formulate an outcome

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: triggers, beneficial ownership, cross-border risk
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:

- Session 1: Change-of-control triggers and criteria (09:30–10:45)

- Session 3: Cross-border ownership and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how supervisory authorities cooperate with criminal prosecutors and other enforcement bodies, including managing parallel proceedings and information-sharing gateways.

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Criminal referral and information gateways (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain referral circumstances and information gateways*
- When criminal referral is appropriate versus civil enforcement
- Statutory information-sharing gateways with prosecutors
- Confidentiality and legal privilege considerations in sharing information
- Building working relationships with prosecutorial authorities
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: referral experiences from participants' own jurisdictions

**Session 2: Managing parallel proceedings (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess the challenges of parallel proceedings*
- Coordinating timing between civil enforcement and criminal proceedings
- Managing the risk of prejudicing a criminal case
- Stay of civil proceedings pending criminal outcome
- Case examples of parallel proceedings management
Activities:
- Group exercise: sequence civil and criminal proceedings for a sample case

**Session 3: Multi-authority cooperation and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate cooperation arrangements and formulate a strategy*
- Cooperation with domestic authorities (police, tax, FIU)
- Cooperation with foreign prosecutorial authorities
- Case study: a case requiring coordination across multiple authorities
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a multi-authority cooperation strategy for a sample case

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: referral, information gateways, parallel proceedings, cooperation
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in communicating effectively in cross-border supervisory contexts, including supervisory colleges and international cooperation frameworks, recognising cultural differences in communication style and expectations.

Activities:

*Objective: Identify style differences and apply clear communication techniques*
- Communication style differences relevant to supervisory colleges
- Techniques for clarity across language barriers

- Written versus spoken communication considerations
Activities:
- Group exercise: identify communication risks in a sample multinational college discussion

**Session 3: Managing miscommunication risk and practice (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess miscommunication risk and practise communication*
- Assessing where miscommunication risk is highest in international cooperation
- Checking understanding without causing offence
- Case study: a cross-border miscommunication and its consequences
Activities:
- Role-play: a cross-cultural supervisory college discussion

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: cultural effects, style differences, managing risk
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of data governance principles and their application to supervisory decision-making, ensuring that decisions are supported by reliable, well-governed data.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-to-senior staff involved in the authority's own data and technology infrastructure.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the principles of good data governance
- Describe common data quality issues affecting supervisory decisions
- Assess data lineage and its importance for defensible decisions
- Evaluate the governance of decision-support systems
- Formulate data governance improvements for a sample scenario
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Principles of data governance (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain data governance principles*
- What data governance means for a supervisory authority
- Data ownership, stewardship, and accountability
- Data quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, timeliness
- Consequences of poor data governance for supervisory decisions
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: data quality issues participants have encountered

**Session 2: Data lineage and decision defensibility (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess data lineage and its role in defensible decisions*
- What data lineage is and why it matters
- Tracing a supervisory decision back to its underlying data
- Governance of decision-support and analytics systems
- Documenting data provenance for audit and challenge
Activities:
- Exercise: trace the data lineage behind a sample supervisory decision

**Session 3: Applying data governance (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Formulate governance improvements for a scenario*
- Common data governance weaknesses in supervisory authorities
- Practical steps to strengthen data governance
- Case study: a decision challenged due to poor data governance
Activities:
- Case study: propose data governance improvements for a sample authority

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: governance principles, lineage, applying improvements
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Principles of data governance (09:30–10:45)

- Session 3: Applying data governance (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Good data governance is a precondition for defensible supervisory decisions, not a bureaucratic add-on
- Data lineage lets an authority show its working when a decision is challenged
- Decision-support systems need the same governance rigour as the decisions they inform

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in applying a sanctioning framework consistently, weighing aggravating and mitigating factors and maintaining consistency with precedent while addressing the specific facts of a case.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level enforcement investigators and case officers.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the purpose of sanctions within the enforcement toolkit
- Apply a structured sanctioning framework to a case
- Weigh aggravating and mitigating factors systematically
- Assess consistency with precedent when determining a sanction
- Formulate a proportionate sanction for a sample case
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: The purpose of sanctions (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the purpose of sanctions*
- Sanctions as deterrence, punishment, and market signalling
- Types of sanction: financial penalties, restrictions, public censure
- Proportionality as the guiding sanctioning principle
- The role of published sanctioning guidelines
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: sanctioning approaches from participants' own jurisdictions

**Session 2: Sanctioning frameworks in practice (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Apply a sanctioning framework and weigh aggravating/mitigating factors*
- Structured sanctioning frameworks: seriousness, harm, culpability
- Aggravating factors: repeat conduct, concealment, senior involvement
- Mitigating factors: self-reporting, remediation, cooperation
- Financial penalty calculation methodologies
Activities:
- Group exercise: apply a sanctioning framework to a sample case

**Session 3: Precedent and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess consistency with precedent and formulate a sanction*
- Using precedent to maintain sanctioning consistency
- Distinguishing genuinely comparable cases from superficially similar ones
- Case study: determining a sanction for a sample enforcement case
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a proportionate sanction, referencing precedent

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: purpose, framework, aggravating/mitigating factors, precedent
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: The purpose of sanctions (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Sanctioning frameworks in practice (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Precedent and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Proportionate sanctioning balances the specific facts of a case against the need for overall consistency
- A structured framework prevents sanctioning decisions from becoming arbitrary or unpredictable
- Precedent should guide, not mechanically dictate, the sanction in a new case

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' ability to recognise early warning signs of firm distress and apply a structured intervention ladder before problems become crises.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-to-senior staff involved in crisis preparedness, recovery, and resolution planning.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the concept of an intervention ladder
- Identify common early warning indicators of firm distress
- Assess when escalation up the intervention ladder is warranted
- Apply structured decision thresholds for early intervention
- Formulate an early intervention response for a sample scenario
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Warning signs and the intervention ladder (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the intervention ladder concept*
- The intervention ladder: from monitoring to formal action
- Why early intervention is more effective than late intervention
- Common early warning indicators across risk types
- Behavioural versus quantitative warning signs
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: early warning signs participants have observed

**Session 2: Escalation thresholds (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess escalation triggers and apply decision thresholds*
- Deciding when to escalate up the intervention ladder
- Balancing false alarms against late intervention risk
- Structured decision thresholds for common warning signs
- Documenting the basis for escalation decisions
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample firm's warning signs and decide on an escalation point

**Session 3: Applying early intervention (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Formulate an early intervention response*
- Options available at each rung of the intervention ladder
- Case study: a firm showing early signs of distress
Activities:
- Case study: formulate an early intervention response for a sample firm

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: warning signs, escalation thresholds, intervention
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Warning signs and the intervention ladder (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Escalation thresholds (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Applying early intervention (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Early intervention is almost always more effective and less costly than late intervention
- A structured intervention ladder makes escalation decisions consistent and defensible
- Behavioural warning signs often precede quantitative deterioration and deserve equal attention

*Objective: Explain sources of bias in financial crime AI*

- Regulatory and ethical expectations around fairness
Activities:

**Session 2: Testing for bias (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Apply bias-testing techniques*
- Techniques for testing AI systems for bias against protected characteristics
- Interpreting bias-testing results
- Remediation options when bias is identified
- Limitations of bias-testing methodologies
Activities:
- Group exercise: interpret sample bias-testing results for a financial crime AI system

**Session 3: Accountability and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate accountability and formulate an assessment*
- Audit trail requirements for AI-driven decisions
- Human-in-the-loop safeguards and their design
- Case study: a bias concern identified in a firm's AI system
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of bias risk and recommend safeguards

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: bias sources, testing, accountability, safeguards
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in gathering and preserving evidence to a standard suitable for enforcement or court proceedings, including disclosure obligations and maintaining a defensible evidential record.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level enforcement investigators and case officers.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the evidential standards required for enforcement action
- Describe disclosure obligations during an investigation
- Apply techniques for maintaining a defensible chain of custody

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Evidential standards (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain evidential standards and disclosure obligations*
- Evidential standards required for enforcement versus supervisory action
- Disclosure obligations to the subject of an investigation

Activities:

**Session 2: Chain of custody and evidence preservation (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Apply chain-of-custody techniques*
- Maintaining a defensible chain of custody
- Preserving digital evidence without contamination
- Documenting the provenance of evidence
- Common evidence-handling errors that undermine cases
Activities:

**Session 3: Witness statements and evidence review (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Draft a witness statement and evaluate an evidence file*
- Structuring an evidentially sound witness statement
- Avoiding leading or suggestive statement-taking
- Case study: a case undermined by evidential weaknesses
Activities:
- Case study: draft a witness statement and evaluate a sample evidence file for gaps

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: standards, disclosure, chain of custody, statements
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:

- Session 1: Evidential standards (09:30–10:45)

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in exercising supervisory judgement when information is incomplete or ambiguous, recognising common cognitive biases and applying frameworks that improve consistency and defensibility of decisions.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisory staff developing core professional judgement skills.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain why supervisory judgement is often exercised under genuine uncertainty
- Identify common cognitive biases that affect supervisory decisions
- Apply structured judgement frameworks to reduce inconsistency
- Evaluate the defensibility of a supervisory judgement
- Formulate a well-reasoned judgement for an ambiguous scenario
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Judgement and uncertainty (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the nature of supervisory judgement under uncertainty*
- Why supervision inherently involves judgement calls, not just rule application
- Sources of uncertainty: incomplete information, evolving risk, ambiguous rules
- The cost of both over- and under-cautious judgement
- Judgement versus discretion — what accountability requires
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: judgement calls participants have found genuinely difficult

**Session 2: Cognitive biases in supervisory decisions (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Identify cognitive biases*
- Common biases: confirmation bias, anchoring, groupthink, hindsight bias
- How biases specifically distort supervisory risk assessment
- Techniques for recognising bias in your own reasoning
- Structural safeguards against biased decision-making
Activities:
- Exercise: identify biases at play in a set of sample supervisory decisions

**Session 3: Structured judgement frameworks (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Apply frameworks and evaluate defensibility*
- Structured frameworks for exercising judgement consistently
- Documenting the reasoning behind a judgement for defensibility
- Case study: an ambiguous scenario requiring a reasoned judgement
Activities:
- Case study: formulate and document a judgement for an ambiguous scenario

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: uncertainty, bias, structured frameworks
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Judgement and uncertainty (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Cognitive biases in supervisory decisions (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Structured judgement frameworks (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Supervisory judgement under uncertainty is unavoidable — the goal is consistency and defensibility, not certainty
- Cognitive biases affect experienced supervisors just as much as novices, and awareness is the first defence
- A well-documented reasoning process is what makes a judgement defensible under later scrutiny

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to introduce participants to financial inclusion as a policy and supervisory concern, exploring the barriers that prevent access to financial services and the regulatory tools available to promote inclusive access without compromising other regulatory objectives such as financial crime prevention.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors assessing consumer protection outcomes.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the concept and measurement of financial inclusion
- Identify common barriers to accessing financial services
- Discuss the tension between financial inclusion and financial crime controls
- Evaluate inclusive product design practices
- Assess the role of regulation in promoting or hindering inclusion
- Identify policy options to improve financial inclusion outcomes
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Understanding financial inclusion (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain financial inclusion and its barriers*
- Defining and measuring financial inclusion
- Barriers: cost, access, documentation, trust, digital literacy
- Financial inclusion as a supervisory and policy concern
- Global perspectives on inclusion initiatives
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: barriers to access in participants' own markets

**Session 2: Inclusion versus other regulatory objectives (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Discuss the tension between inclusion and financial crime controls*
- The 'de-risking' problem: how AML/CFT controls can restrict access
- Balancing proportionate financial crime controls with inclusion
- Inclusive product design: simplified accounts, tiered KYC
- International examples of proportionate approaches
Activities:
- Group discussion: designing a proportionate KYC regime for a basic account product

**Session 3: Policy options and supervisory role (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess regulatory levers and identify policy options*
- The supervisor's role in promoting inclusion
- Policy levers: proportionality, guidance, innovation hubs
- Measuring progress on financial inclusion
- Case study: an inclusion initiative and its outcomes
Activities:
- Case study exercise: assess an inclusion initiative and propose improvements

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: barriers, tensions, policy options
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

- Ensuring consistent decisions across similar cases

sectionHtml.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how a supervisory authority makes rules, covering the legal hierarchy between primary legislation, secondary rules, and guidance, and the core principles of clear, enforceable regulatory drafting.
sectionHtml.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level policy officers drafting or contributing to rules, guidance, and consultation papers.
sectionHtml.Learning Objectives:
• Explain the legal hierarchy of primary legislation, secondary rules and guidance
  • Describe the sources of rule-making power for a supervisory authority
  • Apply principles of clear, enforceable regulatory drafting
  • Distinguish between binding rules and non-binding guidance
  • Identify common drafting pitfalls that create ambiguity or unintended loopholes
  • Evaluate a draft rule against clarity and enforceability criteria
sectionHtml.Syllabus:
Session 1: The legal hierarchy of rule-making (09:30–10:45)

*Objective: Explain the legal hierarchy and sources of rule-making power*

  • Primary legislation, secondary rules, and guidance: what each can and cannot do
  • Sources of a supervisory authority's rule-making power
  • Delegated powers and their limits
  • Binding rules versus non-binding guidance

Activities:

  • Facilitated discussion: mapping the rule-making hierarchy in participants' own jurisdictions

Session 2: Principles of clear drafting (11:00–12:30)

*Objective: Apply drafting principles and identify common pitfalls*

  • Principles of clear, enforceable regulatory drafting
  • Common drafting pitfalls: ambiguity, loopholes, inconsistent definitions
  • Drafting for different audiences: firms, courts, the public
  • The role of legal review in the drafting process

Activities:

  • Exercise: redraft a poorly worded sample rule for clarity

Session 3: Evaluating draft rules (13:30–14:45)

*Objective: Evaluate a draft rule against clarity and enforceability criteria*

  • Criteria for assessing draft rules
  • Testing rules against real-world scenarios before finalisation
  • Case study: a rule that caused unintended consequences due to poor drafting

Activities:

  • Case study: evaluate a draft rule and propose improvements

Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

*Objective: Consolidate learning*

  • Recap: hierarchy, drafting principles, evaluation

Activities:

  • Reflection and discussion
  • Q&A

Activities:

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of a supervisory authority's enforcement function — what powers exist, how the decision to open an investigation is made, and how cases are triaged and prioritised.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level enforcement investigators and case officers.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the range of enforcement powers available to a supervisory authority
- Describe the criteria used to decide whether to open an investigation
- Apply a case triage framework to prioritise enforcement matters
- Distinguish enforcement from ongoing supervisory intervention
- Evaluate the resourcing implications of an enforcement caseload
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Enforcement powers and purpose (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the range of enforcement powers*
- Types of enforcement power: investigative, sanctioning, remedial
- The purpose of enforcement within the broader supervisory toolkit
- Distinguishing enforcement from ongoing supervisory intervention
- Statutory thresholds for opening an investigation
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: enforcement's role relative to supervision in participants' own authorities

**Session 2: Deciding to investigate (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe investigation criteria and apply a triage framework*
- Criteria for deciding whether to open an investigation
- Case triage: severity, evidential strength, public interest
- Balancing enforcement priorities against limited resource
- Escalation routes from supervision into enforcement
Activities:
- Group exercise: triage a set of sample cases for investigation priority

**Session 3: Resourcing and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate resourcing implications and apply learning to a scenario*
- Resourcing an enforcement caseload: skills, time, external support
- Managing a growing or backlogged caseload
- Case study: a resourcing-constrained enforcement decision
Activities:
- Case study: propose a triage and resourcing plan for a sample caseload

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: powers, investigation decisions, triage, resourcing
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

**Session 1: Purpose of liquidity stress testing (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the purpose of liquidity stress testing*

*Objective: Assess liquidity management tools and formulate a supervisory view*
- Liquidity management tools: swing pricing, redemption gates, suspension
- Assessing whether tools are calibrated and usable in practice
- Case study: a fund's liquidity stress-testing framework under review
Activities:
- Case study: assess a sample fund's liquidity stress-testing framework and formulate a supervisory view

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: purpose, guidelines, redemption modelling, liquidity tools
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Purpose of liquidity stress testing (09:30–10:45)

- Session 3: Liquidity management tools and application (13:30–14:45)

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how fund managers structure delegation and outsourcing arrangements, and how supervisors assess effective oversight of third-party arrangements.

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Delegation and outsourcing regulation (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the delegation regulatory framework*
- Why delegation and outsourcing are common in fund management
- Regulatory framework governing delegation (AIFMD, UCITS)
- Distinguishing delegation from outsourcing

Activities:

**Session 2: Assessing effective oversight (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess whether managers retain effective oversight*
- Criteria for assessing effective oversight of a delegate
- Common weaknesses: inadequate monitoring, resource gaps at the manager
- Reviewing service level agreements and oversight reporting
- Red flags indicating a manager has lost effective control
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample delegation arrangement for effective oversight

**Session 3: Concentration risk and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Identify concentration/continuity risk and formulate an assessment*
- Concentration risk from reliance on a small number of key service providers
- Business continuity considerations for outsourced functions
- Case study: a manager's outsourcing framework under review
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of a manager's outsourcing framework

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: delegation framework, effective oversight, concentration risk
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build supervisors' ability to assess how firms identify and respond to customer vulnerability. Participants will learn the drivers of vulnerability, how firms should adapt products, communications and service for vulnerable customers, and how to assess whether a firm's vulnerable-customer framework is effective in practice rather than just on paper.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors assessing consumer protection outcomes.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the drivers and dimensions of customer vulnerability
- Describe regulatory expectations for identifying vulnerable customers
- Assess the adequacy of a firm's vulnerable-customer policy
- Evaluate whether frontline staff are equipped to identify vulnerability
- Analyse case examples of tailored treatment for vulnerable customers
- Identify gaps between a firm's stated policy and its practical delivery
- Formulate supervisory conclusions on vulnerable-customer treatment
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Understanding vulnerability (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain the drivers and dimensions of vulnerability*
- Drivers of vulnerability: health, life events, resilience, capability
- Vulnerability as a spectrum, not a fixed category
- Regulatory expectations for identifying vulnerable customers
- The business case for good vulnerable-customer practice
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: how vulnerability shows up in different sectors
- Exercise: map vulnerability drivers to customer scenarios

**Session 2: Assessing firm frameworks (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess the adequacy of a firm's vulnerable-customer policy and frontline delivery*
- What a good vulnerable-customer policy contains
- Frontline identification: training, tools, escalation routes
- Tailoring products, communications and service
- Common weaknesses in practice versus policy
Activities:
- Group exercise: review a sample vulnerable-customer policy
- Role-play: a frontline interaction with a vulnerable customer

**Session 3: Case examples and supervisory assessment (13:30–15:00)**
*Objective: Apply learning to case examples and form supervisory judgements*
- Case examples of good and poor tailored treatment
- Identifying the gap between stated policy and delivery
- Supervisory tools for assessing vulnerable-customer outcomes
- Escalation and intervention where practice falls short
Activities:
- Case study: assess a firm's vulnerable-customer framework and produce supervisory conclusions

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (15:00–15:15)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: vulnerability drivers, policy assessment, practical delivery
- Reinforcing the spectrum view of vulnerability
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Understanding vulnerability (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Assessing firm frameworks (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Case examples and supervisory assessment (13:30–15:00)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (15:00–15:15)

**Key Takeaways**
- Vulnerability is a spectrum that can affect any customer, not a fixed group
- A good policy is meaningless without frontline capability to act on it
- Supervisors should test delivery in practice, not just review documentation

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to deepen participants' understanding of issuer disclosure as a core investor-protection mechanism, drawing on IOSCO's Principles for Issuers, and to build practical skills in assessing whether disclosure practices are full, accurate, and timely.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors assessing consumer protection outcomes.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the role of disclosure in protecting investors
- Describe IOSCO's Principles for Issuers and their disclosure requirements
- Assess whether disclosure is full, accurate and timely
- Evaluate the quality of financial and non-financial disclosures
- Identify red flags in issuer disclosure practices
- Formulate supervisory conclusions on disclosure adequacy
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Disclosure as investor protection (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain why disclosure matters as an investor-protection tool*
- IOSCO's investor-protection objective and the role of disclosure
- The Principles for Issuers: full, accurate and timely disclosure
- Financial versus non-financial disclosure
- Consequences of disclosure failures for investors and markets
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: notable disclosure failures and their investor impact

**Session 2: Assessing disclosure quality (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess whether disclosure meets the full/accurate/timely standard*
- Frameworks for assessing disclosure completeness and accuracy
- Timeliness expectations and common failure points
- Assessing narrative versus quantitative disclosure
- The role of auditors and gatekeepers
Activities:
- Group exercise: review a sample issuer disclosure against the full/accurate/timely standard

**Session 3: Red flags and supervisory application (13:30–15:00)**
*Objective: Identify red flags and form supervisory conclusions*
- Common red flags in issuer disclosure
- Linking disclosure weaknesses to wider governance or business model risk
- Supervisory tools for challenging inadequate disclosure
- Case study: a disclosure red flag scenario
Activities:
- Case study: analyse an issuer's disclosure and produce a supervisory assessment

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (15:00–15:15)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: disclosure as protection, quality assessment, red flags
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Disclosure as investor protection (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Assessing disclosure quality (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Red flags and supervisory application (13:30–15:00)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (15:00–15:15)

**Key Takeaways**
- Disclosure is one of the most direct mechanisms by which regulation protects investors
- Full, accurate and timely disclosure is a single standard with three distinct failure modes
- Disclosure red flags are often the earliest visible sign of deeper governance problems

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in designing systems and practices that preserve institutional knowledge and supervisory precedent despite staff turnover.
sections.Intended Audience: Managers and learning & development leads responsible for building supervisory capability within the authority.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the risks that staff turnover poses to institutional memory
- Describe knowledge management approaches suited to supervisory work
- Assess the adequacy of a case precedent system
- Evaluate handover practices for departing staff
- Formulate a knowledge management improvement plan
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Institutional memory and turnover risk (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain turnover risk to institutional memory*
- Why supervisory judgement depends heavily on tacit institutional knowledge
- The cost of losing precedent and context when staff leave
- Common knowledge management failure modes in regulatory bodies
- Balancing documentation burden against knowledge preservation needs
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: knowledge loss episodes participants have experienced

**Session 2: Knowledge management approaches (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe approaches and assess precedent systems*
- Approaches: case precedent databases, communities of practice, mentoring
- Designing an accessible, searchable case precedent system
- Balancing formal systems against informal knowledge networks
- Assessing whether a precedent system is actually used
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample case precedent system for usability and completeness

**Session 3: Handover practices and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate handover practices and formulate an improvement plan*
- Good practice in staff handover and offboarding
- Capturing tacit knowledge before it is lost
- Case study: a knowledge gap discovered after a departure
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a knowledge management improvement plan for a sample authority

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: turnover risk, knowledge management approaches, handover practice
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Institutional memory and turnover risk (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Knowledge management approaches (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Handover practices and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Supervisory judgement depends heavily on institutional memory that is easily lost through turnover
- A precedent system only has value if it is genuinely used, not just maintained
- Good handover practice should be a deliberate discipline, not left to individual goodwill

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of systemic risk and contagion channels, and the macroprudential tools available to address them.
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-to-senior staff involved in crisis preparedness, recovery, and resolution planning.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the concept of systemic risk and its distinguishing features
- Describe common contagion channels between firms and markets
- Identify systemic risk indicators relevant to a supervisory authority
- Assess the macroprudential tools available to address systemic risk
- Evaluate a scenario for systemic risk and propose a policy response
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Understanding systemic risk (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain systemic risk and its features*
- What distinguishes systemic risk from firm-specific risk
- Interconnectedness, size, and substitutability as systemic risk drivers
- Historical episodes of systemic risk crystallising
- The evolving perimeter of systemic risk beyond banks
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: systemic risk episodes participants have studied or observed

**Session 2: Contagion channels and indicators (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe contagion channels and identify indicators*
- Contagion channels: direct exposure, fire sales, confidence effects
- Systemic risk indicators used by supervisory authorities
- Data challenges in monitoring systemic risk
- Cross-border dimensions of contagion
Activities:
- Group exercise: map contagion channels for a sample interconnected market

**Session 3: Macroprudential tools and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess macroprudential tools and propose a policy response*
- Macroprudential tools: capital buffers, liquidity requirements, exposure limits
- Matching tools to specific systemic risk drivers
- Case study: a scenario with emerging systemic risk
Activities:
- Case study: assess a systemic risk scenario and propose a macroprudential policy response

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: systemic risk features, contagion channels, macroprudential tools
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Understanding systemic risk (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Contagion channels and indicators (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Macroprudential tools and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Systemic risk is fundamentally about interconnectedness, not just the size of any single firm
- Contagion can spread through confidence effects as fast as through direct financial exposure
- Macroprudential tools need to be matched deliberately to the specific systemic risk driver they address

- Interconnectedness risk between infrastructure entities
Activities:

**Session 3: Risk management and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate risk management and formulate an assessment*
- Assessing default management and margining arrangements
- Operational resilience considerations for market infrastructure
- Case study: a market infrastructure entity under supervisory review

- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in designing and using metrics that meaningfully measure supervisory effectiveness and outcomes, drawing on approaches used in international assessments such as IMF/World Bank Financial Sector Assessment Programs (FSAPs).
sections.Intended Audience: Mid-to-senior supervisory staff involved in setting or reviewing their authority's strategy, governance, or resourcing decisions.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain why measuring supervisory effectiveness is difficult
- Describe approaches used in international assessments such as FSAPs
- Distinguish output metrics from outcome metrics
- Design a balanced set of effectiveness metrics for a supervisory function
- Evaluate the risks of poorly designed metrics
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: The challenge of measuring effectiveness (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain why effectiveness measurement is difficult*
- Why supervisory effectiveness resists simple measurement
- Output metrics versus outcome metrics
- The risk of measuring what's easy rather than what matters
- International approaches: FSAP assessment methodology
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: metrics currently used in participants' own authorities

**Session 2: Designing balanced metrics (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Distinguish metric types and design a balanced set*
- Distinguishing output, process and outcome metrics
- Balancing quantitative and qualitative indicators
- Benchmarking against international peers
- Avoiding perverse incentives from poorly designed metrics
Activities:
- Group exercise: design a balanced metrics scorecard for a supervisory function

**Session 3: Risks and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate metric design risks and apply to a case study*
- Common metric design failures
- Gaming and unintended consequences of poor metrics
- Case study: a metrics framework and its unintended effects
Activities:
- Case study: critique a sample metrics framework and propose improvements

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: measurement challenges, metric design, risks
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:

- Effectiveness metrics should measure outcomes, not just activity levels

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of how money market funds are regulated under the MMFR and the systemic risk considerations that drive regulatory reform, and the supervisory tools used to assess MMF resilience.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors working in investment funds supervision.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the role and structure of money market funds
- Describe the key requirements of the Money Market Fund Regulation (MMFR)
- Assess the systemic risk posed by money market funds
- Evaluate NAV stability mechanisms and their limitations
- Formulate a supervisory assessment of an MMF's resilience
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: MMFs and their regulation (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain MMF structure and describe the MMFR*
- The role of money market funds in short-term funding markets
- Types of MMF: public debt CNAV, LVNAV, VNAV
- Key MMFR requirements: liquidity buffers, stress testing, reporting
- Why MMFs attracted post-crisis regulatory reform
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: MMF stress episodes participants are aware of

**Session 2: Systemic risk and NAV stability (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess systemic risk and evaluate NAV stability mechanisms*
- Why MMFs are considered systemically significant
- Run risk and first-mover advantage in MMF redemptions
- NAV stability mechanisms and their limitations under stress
- Ongoing international reform debates (e.g. swing pricing for MMFs)
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess the run risk profile of a sample MMF structure

**Session 3: Supervisory assessment and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Formulate a resilience assessment*
- Supervisory tools for assessing MMF resilience
- Reviewing stress-test results and liquidity buffer adequacy
- Case study: an MMF facing redemption pressure
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of a sample MMF's resilience

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: MMF structure, MMFR, systemic risk, NAV stability
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: MMFs and their regulation (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Systemic risk and NAV stability (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Supervisory assessment and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Money market funds sit at the intersection of fund regulation and systemic risk, requiring both lenses
- First-mover redemption advantage is the core structural vulnerability the MMFR seeks to address
- NAV stability mechanisms reduce but do not eliminate run risk under sufficiently severe stress

sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisors working in payment services supervision.

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Understanding APP fraud (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain APP fraud characteristics*
- What distinguishes authorised push payment fraud from unauthorised fraud
- Common APP fraud scenarios: impersonation, invoice fraud, romance scams
- Why APP fraud has grown alongside faster payment methods
- The psychological techniques used in APP scams
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: APP fraud trends participants have observed

**Session 2: Liability allocation and prevention controls (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe liability frameworks and assess prevention controls*
- Liability allocation frameworks for APP scam losses between sending and receiving firms
- Confirmation of payee and other preventive control mechanisms
- Assessing whether a firm's warnings and friction points are effective without being excessive
- International approaches to APP fraud liability
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample firm's APP fraud prevention controls

**Session 3: Fraud reporting and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate fraud reporting data and formulate an assessment*
- Using fraud reporting data as a supervisory early-warning tool
- Assessing data quality and consistency in fraud reporting
- Case study: a firm's APP fraud framework under supervisory review
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a supervisory assessment of a firm's APP fraud prevention framework

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: APP fraud characteristics, liability allocation, prevention and reporting
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Understanding APP fraud (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Liability allocation and prevention controls (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Fraud reporting and application (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- APP fraud exploits authorised payment authorisation itself, making it structurally different from traditional unauthorised fraud

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of the principles of procedural fairness that must be applied in enforcement decision-making, including the right to make representations and managing conflicts of interest.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level enforcement investigators and case officers.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the principles of natural justice as applied to enforcement
- Describe the right to make representations and how it is given effect
- Identify and manage conflicts of interest in enforcement decision-making
- Assess whether a decision-making process meets procedural fairness standards
- Formulate a fair process design for a sample enforcement case
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Principles of natural justice (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain natural justice principles*
- The two pillars of natural justice: right to be heard, freedom from bias
- How natural justice applies specifically to enforcement decisions
- Consequences of procedural unfairness for enforcement outcomes
- International and domestic case law touchpoints
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: procedural fairness challenges participants have encountered

**Session 2: Representations and conflicts of interest (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Describe representation rights and manage conflicts of interest*
- Giving effect to the right to make representations
- Timelines and format for representations
- Identifying conflicts of interest in the decision-making chain
- Structural separation between investigation and decision functions
Activities:
- Group exercise: identify conflicts of interest in a sample decision-making structure

**Session 3: Assessing and designing fair process (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Assess fairness and design a fair process*
- Criteria for assessing procedural fairness of a process
- Designing a fair process from the outset rather than retrofitting
- Case study: a decision challenged on procedural fairness grounds
Activities:
- Case study: design a procedurally fair decision-making process for a sample case

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: natural justice, representations, conflicts of interest
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Principles of natural justice (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Representations and conflicts of interest (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Assessing and designing fair process (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Procedural fairness is not a technicality — unfair process can invalidate an otherwise justified enforcement outcome
- Structural separation between investigation and decision-making is one of the strongest safeguards against bias
- Building fairness into a process design from the outset is far more effective than correcting it after challenge

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in assessing the credibility of firms' recovery plans and understanding the supervisor's role in resolution planning and resolvability assessment.

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Recovery versus resolution (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain recovery and resolution concepts*
- Recovery planning: firm-led actions to restore viability
- Resolution planning: authority-led actions if recovery fails
- Why the distinction matters for supervisory role clarity
- International standards on recovery and resolution planning
Activities:

**Session 2: Assessing recovery plan credibility (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Assess recovery plan credibility*
- Criteria for assessing recovery plan credibility
- Common weaknesses: unrealistic assumptions, untested options
- Assessing recovery options against a range of stress scenarios
- The role of recovery plan testing and dry-runs
Activities:
- Group exercise: assess a sample recovery plan's credibility

**Session 3: Resolution planning and resolvability (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Describe the resolution planning role and evaluate resolvability*
- The supervisor/resolution authority's role in resolution planning
- Assessing resolvability barriers: structure, data, continuity of services
- Case study: a firm with significant resolvability barriers
Activities:
- Case study: evaluate resolvability barriers and formulate a supervisory view

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: recovery/resolution distinction, credibility, resolvability
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Recovery versus resolution (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Assessing recovery plan credibility (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Resolution planning and resolvability (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Recovery and resolution planning serve different purposes and require different supervisory lenses

*Objective: Explain key risk categories*

- Verifying safeguarding through reconciliation and audit evidence
- Consequences of safeguarding failure for consumers
Activities:

*Objective: Evaluate resilience indicators and formulate an assessment*
- Operational and financial resilience indicators for payment institutions
- Case study: a payment institution's risk profile under supervisory review
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a risk-based supervisory assessment of a sample payment institution

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: risk categories, safeguarding assessment, resilience indicators
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in designing and applying a risk-based supervisory approach that allocates limited supervisory resource to the areas of greatest risk, addressing the common challenge of unclear mandates and resource constraints.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level supervisory staff conducting day-to-day risk assessment and firm engagement.

- Evaluate resource allocation decisions against risk priorities

sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Principles of risk-based supervision (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain risk-based supervision principles*
- Why risk-based supervision replaced compliance-based approaches
- Risk appetite frameworks for supervisory authorities
- The relationship between risk appetite and resource allocation
- International practice on risk-based supervisory models
Activities:

**Session 2: Supervisory intensity models (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Apply a risk appetite framework and assess intensity models*
- Models for varying supervisory intensity by risk tier
- Trade-offs: breadth of coverage versus depth of scrutiny
- Dynamic reprioritisation as risks change
- Tools for structured resource allocation
Activities:
- Group exercise: design a supervisory intensity model for a sample population of firms

**Session 3: Resource allocation and application (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Evaluate resource allocation and formulate a work plan*
- Evaluating whether resource allocation matches stated risk priorities
- Managing stakeholder expectations when resource is constrained
- Case study: reprioritising a supervisory work plan mid-year
Activities:
- Case study: formulate a risk-based work plan under a constrained resource scenario

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: principles, intensity models, resource allocation
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A

sections.Aim and Purpose: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in designing and running an effective public consultation on proposed rules, including stakeholder engagement strategy and how to analyse and respond to consultation feedback transparently.
sections.Intended Audience: Junior to mid-level policy officers drafting or contributing to rules, guidance, and consultation papers.
sections.Learning Objectives:
- Explain the purpose and value of regulatory consultation
- Design an effective consultation process and timeline
- Develop a stakeholder engagement strategy for a consultation
- Apply techniques for analysing consultation responses systematically
- Draft a transparent feedback statement responding to consultation input
sections.Syllabus:
**Session 1: Purpose and design of consultation (09:30–10:45)**
*Objective: Explain consultation purpose and design an effective process*
- Why consultation improves rule quality and legitimacy
- Designing a consultation timeline and document
- Consultation questions: open versus closed, avoiding leading questions
- Statutory versus voluntary consultation requirements
Activities:
- Facilitated discussion: consultation experiences, good and bad, from participants

**Session 2: Stakeholder engagement strategy (11:00–12:30)**
*Objective: Develop a stakeholder engagement strategy*
- Identifying and mapping consultation stakeholders
- Engagement channels: written responses, roundtables, targeted outreach
- Ensuring smaller or less-resourced stakeholders are heard
- Balancing industry input against other public interests
Activities:
- Group exercise: design a stakeholder engagement plan for a sample consultation

**Session 3: Analysing and responding to feedback (13:30–14:45)**
*Objective: Analyse consultation responses and draft a feedback statement*
- Systematic approaches to analysing consultation responses
- Identifying themes versus outlier views
- Drafting a transparent feedback statement
- Handling contentious or high-volume responses
Activities:
- Exercise: analyse a set of sample consultation responses and draft key feedback points

**Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)**
*Objective: Consolidate learning*
- Recap: purpose, design, stakeholder engagement, feedback analysis
Activities:
- Reflection and discussion
- Q&A
sections.Structure and Format:
Proposed as a half-day workshop (approx. 3.5 hours substantive content), comprising 4 sessions:
- Session 1: Purpose and design of consultation (09:30–10:45)
- Session 2: Stakeholder engagement strategy (11:00–12:30)
- Session 3: Analysing and responding to feedback (13:30–14:45)
- Session 4: Wrap-up and key takeaways (14:45–15:00)

**Key Takeaways**
- Good consultation design shapes the quality of the input an authority receives
- Stakeholder engagement should actively seek out less-resourced voices, not just respond to the loudest
- A transparent feedback statement builds trust even when not every response can be accommodated
